teaching.causalExplanation: Watch. One cone of water fills the cylinder a third of the way. Two cones, two thirds. And three cones fill it exactly. So a cone holds a third of the cylinder with the same base and height. The pour shows it for this cone, and it's been proved for any cone and its matching cylinder, big or small. It's always three. Why less than half? Remember the slice stack from last time. For a cylinder, every slice is the same circle. But a cone's slices shrink all the way to a point at the top, the apex, so most of its volume is down near the base, and the narrow top holds very little. Here, the cylinder is pi times three squared times ten, ninety pi. A third of that is thirty pi, about ninety-four point two five cubic centimetres. So for a cone, the volume is a third, times the area of the base, times the height. A pyramid is a solid with a flat base, whose sides slope up to meet at a point. A cone is really just a pyramid with a circle for a base. The same rule works for every one of them. A glass skylight is shaped like a pyramid, one point two metres square at the base and nought point nine of a metre high. The box around it would hold one point two times one point two times nought point nine. The pyramid holds a third of that. A third of one point four four times nought point nine is nought point four three two cubic metres of air under the glass. Every solid that comes to a point holds a third of the prism around it. It doesn't matter whether the base is a square, a rectangle, a triangle or a circle. The height in that formula is the perpendicular height, straight down from the apex at right angles to the base. Sometimes a question gives you the slant height instead, the length along the sloping side. A cone-shaped garden planter has a base radius of thirty centimetres, and its sloping side is fifty centimetres long. The radius, the height and the slope make a right-angled triangle, with the slope as the hypotenuse. So the height is the square root of fifty squared minus thirty squared, forty centimetres. Now the volume is a third, times pi times thirty squared, times forty. That's twelve thousand pi, about thirty-seven thousand seven hundred cubic centimetres, or thirty-seven point seven litres of potting mix. Using fifty as the height is the slip. That's the sloping side, not the height.

## Decisions

- **Anchor: how many cones fill the cylinder? (a09's final frame).** Most students guess two. The pour simulation answers three, exactly, and the ⅓ follows.
- **Why not V = Ah (a09's slice stack, broken).** A cone's slices shrink to a point, so "end × length" overcounts. The shrinking stack is shown beside a09's steady one.
- **Pyramids follow the same rule.** "Any solid that comes to a point, the apex, holds a third of the prism with the same base and height." A skylight pyramid sits inside its box.
- **Perpendicular height (a06).** The height runs straight down from the apex at right angles to the base. If only the slant height is given, a06's Pythagoras finds the height (the cone planter: 30, 40, 50).
- **The sphere as two thirds of its cylinder.** A watermelon fits snugly inside a cylinder as tall as it is wide; it fills two thirds of it: ⅔ × πr² × 2r = 4/3 πr³. The visual comes first; the formula follows.
- **Composite solids by a part list (a08's face list as parts).** The ice cream: cone plus hemisphere scoop.

scenes.teachingReason: Watch. One cone of water fills the cylinder a third of the way. Two cones, two thirds. And three cones fill it exactly. So a cone holds a third of the cylinder with the same base and height. The pour shows it for this cone, and it's been proved for any cone and its matching cylinder, big or small. It's always three. Why less than half? Remember the slice stack from last time. For a cylinder, every slice is the same circle. But a cone's slices shrink all the way to a point at the top, the apex, so most of its volume is down near the base, and the narrow top holds very little. Here, the cylinder is pi times three squared times ten, ninety pi. A third of that is thirty pi, about ninety-four point two five cubic centimetres. So for a cone, the volume is a third, times the area of the base, times the height.

scenes.teachingReason: A pyramid is a solid with a flat base, whose sides slope up to meet at a point. A cone is really just a pyramid with a circle for a base. The same rule works for every one of them. A glass skylight is shaped like a pyramid, one point two metres square at the base and nought point nine of a metre high. A third of one point four four times nought point nine is nought point four three two cubic metres of air under the glass. Every solid that comes to a point holds a third of the prism around it. It doesn't matter whether the base is a square, a rectangle, a triangle or a circle.

scenes.teachingReason: The height in that formula is the perpendicular height, straight down from the apex at right angles to the base. scenes.teachingReason: Spheres have their own rule, and it comes with a surprise. Take a watermelon twenty-four centimetres across, and drop it into a cylinder that fits it snugly, twenty-four across and twenty-four tall. Melons float, so put the lid on to hold it down, then fill the gaps with water. The water that fits around the melon is exactly a third of the cylinder. So the sphere takes up exactly two thirds. Work it through, and two thirds of that cylinder comes out as four thirds, pi, r cubed. That's the sphere's volume. The radius is twelve, so it's four thirds times pi times twelve cubed, about seven thousand two hundred and thirty-eight cubic centimetres. That's seven point two four litres of melon. Notice it's r cubed, not squared, because it's a volume. Half a sphere, a hemisphere, is two thirds pi r cubed.
